title: The Hidden Emotional Cost of Working in Tech
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni writes about the emotional exhaustion that can build in tech careers and argues it is more than ordinary stress. Drawing on Goleman's Primal Leadership, she notes that sustained high pressure pushes people into survival mode and drains the sense of purpose. Her practical responses are a mix of emotional intelligence and Stoicism: tell colleagues and your boss plainly what you are carrying, separate what you can control from what you cannot by drawing two columns, and pause between stimulus and response. She also argues that as AI handles more technical work, human skills like reading a room, building trust and connecting work to human need become more valuable. The piece is personal and informal, but it offers usable habits for leaders and professionals under sustained pressure.
points: Sustained pressure is different from short bursts of stress and can erode purpose, not just energy.
Making your hidden workload visible to your boss and colleagues turns isolation into connection and creates space to finish before taking on more.
A two-column list of what you can control and what you cannot interrupts spiralling and enables strategic rather than reactive responses.
Asking what human need the work serves reconnects technical effort to purpose.
Sustainable excellence rests on showing up as a real person rather than glorifying the grind.
quotes: Although moderate pressure can energize people—the challenge of meeting a deadline, for instance—continued high pressure can be debilitating. As people shift away from pursuing an inspiring vision, pure survival issues take hold,” (Page 73).

This approach isn’t just self-help, it’s ancient Stoic wisdom repackaged for our digital chaos. The Roman philosopher Seneca wrote letters about handling pressure 2,000 years ago that read like they were addressed to burned-out software engineers. The Stoic practice of distinguishing between what we can and cannot control isn’t just philosophical comfort—it’s a practical operating system for your mind when Slack notifications are popping like firecrackers and your project timeline just imploded.

While in a state of absolute stress, I did not always live up to my ideals of leveraging empathy in communication; however, I maintained my professionalism. I was direct and open about what I needed to get through it and how others could assist.

The machines can optimize all day long, but they can’t read a room to save their digital lives. The skills that make us irreplaceable aren’t technical specifications—they’re our ability to build trust, navigate ambiguity, and inspire others through authentic presence.
When I feel lost in the technical weeds, I’ve started a practice of asking: “What human need does this serve?” This simple question reconnects me to purpose when I’m drowning in deployment details.

The tech industry has this obsession with glorifying the grind while sometimes completely ignoring the actual humans making it all run. Sustainable excellence isn’t built on your ability to function on four hours of sleep and cold brew.

When you lead by connecting with people instead of just showcasing your technical wizardry, when you stay steady while everything’s burning down around you, and when you remember there are actual humans on the receiving end of whatever you’re building, that’s when you level up. You don’t just survive the tech hamster wheel; you actually help transform this industry into something that might actually be worth the obscene amount of hours we all put into it.
